cfu-plate-count.formula: CFU/mL = colonies / (dilution_factor * volume_plated). The dilution factor is accepted as a fraction (1e-5) or a times value (100,000) and normalized to the same result.
cfu-plate-count.edition: Per the FDA Bacteriological Analytical Manual (BAM) Chapter 3 (Aerobic Plate Count) and APHA Standard Methods, by name; both public/free.
cfu-plate-count.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
cfu-plate-count.editionNote: Countable range defaults to 15-300 per plate (FDA BAM Chapter 3 since March 2025, as ISO does); APHA uses 25-250, USDA and AOAC 30-300. Counts outside are statistically unreliable (TNTC/TFTC).

assumptions.name: Plated volume
assumptions.value: spread/pour/spiral methods change the effective plated volume

nucleic-acid-a260.formula: concentration = A260 x factor x dilution (factor 50 dsDNA, 33 ssDNA/oligo, 40 RNA, ug/mL per A260); purity_260_280 = A260 / A280.
nucleic-acid-a260.edition: A260 nucleic-acid quantitation (Beer-Lambert at 260 nm; standard spectrophotometric mass factors), by name.
nucleic-acid-a260.freeAccess: Standard molecular-biology spectrophotometry; the mass factors are established practice. The sample and instrument govern.
nucleic-acid-a260.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
nucleic-acid-a260.editionNote: The factor is an empirical mass coefficient, not a molar one, and it differs by strandedness (ssDNA absorbs more per mass, so it reads a lower concentration at the same A260); a 260/280 below about 1.8 (DNA) or 2.0 (RNA) flags protein or phenol carryover that makes the concentration unreliable. Assumes a clean 1 cm path and a blanked instrument. A quantitation aid, not a certified assay.

assumptions.name: Mass extinction factor
assumptions.value: 50 dsDNA / 33 ssDNA, oligo / 40 RNA ug/mL per A260; empirical, not molar

equipment-hourly-rate.formula: deprec = (purchase - salvage)/life_hr; IIT = (iit%/100) x [purchase (N+1) + salvage (N-1)] / (2N) / annual_hr, N = life_hr / annual_hr; owning = deprec + IIT; operating = fuel_gph x price + maint + wear; total = owning + operating.
equipment-hourly-rate.edition: The CAT / AED equipment owning-and-operating cost-recovery method, by name.
equipment-hourly-rate.freeAccess: The owning-and-operating build-up is published in the Caterpillar Performance Handbook and AED cost-recovery guidance. The owner's actual costs, financing, and utilization govern.
equipment-hourly-rate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
equipment-hourly-rate.editionNote: The equipment owning + operating hourly rate: owning = straight-line depreciation (purchase - salvage)/life + the interest/insurance/tax carry (% of the average annual investment [P(N+1) + S(N-1)] / 2N / annual hours, the Caterpillar Performance Handbook Sec. 20 formula; until 2026-09-26 the tile used (P + S) / 2, understating the carry); operating = fuel (gph x price) + maintenance + tires/wear per hour. Running a machine more hours per year spreads the fixed interest-carry thinner, so an idle machine is expensive per hour. This returns the internal cost rate for the entered figures: it uses straight-line depreciation (not a market-value or tax schedule) and the entered annual utilization, and it is a cost-recovery rate, not a rental market rate. A bid-rate aid; the owner's actual costs, financing, and utilization govern.

assumptions.name: Owning
assumptions.value: straight-line depreciation + IIT carry on the average annual investment [P(N+1) + S(N-1)] / 2N / annual hours

assumptions.name: Operating
assumptions.value: fuel (gph x price) + maintenance + tires/wear per hour

assumptions.name: Utilization
assumptions.value: more annual hours spread the fixed carry thinner; a cost rate, not a rental rate

fan-motor-max-airflow.formula: CFM_max = 6356 * BHP * eta_fan / TSP; a motor (nameplate) HP converts to brake HP first with BHP = motor_hp * eta_drive. The inverse of BHP = (CFM * TSP) / (6356 * eta_fan).
fan-motor-max-airflow.edition: AMCA / ASHRAE fan-power relation BHP = (CFM * SP) / (6356 * eta) (public); standard motor HP sizes per NEMA MG 1, by name.
fan-motor-max-airflow.freeAccess: Free principles in published HVAC texts; the 6356 constant is a pure unit derivation.
fan-motor-max-airflow.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed mechanical contractor govern. ACCA Manual J / D / S supersede rules of thumb.
fan-motor-max-airflow.editionNote: The most airflow a fan motor can move against a total static pressure, the inverse of fan-motor-bhp: CFM_max = 6356 * BHP * fan efficiency / TSP, and a nameplate (motor) HP converts to brake HP with the drive efficiency (BHP = motor_hp * eta_drive) because the belt loses a few percent. Airflow falls as the static rises (a dirty filter or throttled damper cuts the CFM at a fixed motor). This is the power ceiling; the actual airflow is where the system curve crosses the fan curve, so treat it as the maximum a motor can support, not a guaranteed delivery. TSP must be the total (external + internal) static at the duty point. Fan curve and motor data govern.

assumptions.name: Power ceiling only
assumptions.value: the delivered airflow is set by the system-curve/fan-curve intersection; this is the max the motor can support

assumptions.name: Total static pressure
assumptions.value: external + internal static at the duty point, not just external

pipe-sizing.formula: WSFU from UPC-style private-use fixture-unit values (above IPC Appendix E Table E103.3(2)); Hunter's Curve converts total WSFU to gpm; DFU per IPC 2021 Table 709.1; supply size from the bundled gpm thresholds; drain size is the smallest IPC 2021 Table 710.1(1) building drain that carries the DFU at the chosen slope, and 3 in minimum with a water closet (Table 709.1 outlet, 704.2).
pipe-sizing.edition: IPC 2021 (International Plumbing Code). Tables 709.1 and 710.1(1) and Appendix E by name; Hunter's Curve (NBS BMS65).
pipe-sizing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed plumber / gas fitter govern. Verify against the IPC / IFGC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
pipe-sizing.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow IPC 2021. Jurisdictions on IPC 2018 / 2024 differ in fixture-unit values and vent-sizing tables; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ. UPC-jurisdictions (CA, IN, MA, NV, parts of NJ) use the Uniform Plumbing Code instead.

assumptions.name: Pressure head at most-distant fixture
assumptions.value: not checked here (IPC 604.6 sets an 8 psi minimum)

assumptions.name: Maximum velocity
assumptions.value: not checked here (8 fps water supply / 5 fps hot water is common practice)

septic-dose-tank.formula: Net dose = daily flow / doses per day; pumped per cycle = net dose + drainback; pumped per day = pumped per cycle x doses; dose-to-void ratio = net dose / distribution-network volume (laterals + manifold; drainback only as a proxy when the network is not entered), target >= 5.
septic-dose-tank.edition: USEPA Onsite Wastewater Treatment Systems Manual (EPA/625/R-00/008); university onsite-wastewater extension low-pressure-pipe design guidance, by name.
septic-dose-tank.freeAccess: Free at epa.gov/septic. Extension LPP design guidance free on land-grant university extension sites.
septic-dose-tank.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed plumber / gas fitter govern. Verify against the IPC / IFGC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
septic-dose-tank.editionNote: Single-edition (EPA manual + extension LPP design guidance, refreshed at build time).

assumptions.name: Default doses per day
assumptions.value: 4 (editable; more, smaller doses rest the soil better)

assumptions.name: Dose-to-void target
assumptions.value: net dose >= 5x the distribution-network volume (laterals plus manifold), not the drainback, so the field pressurizes before the dose is spent

assumptions.name: Drainback handling
assumptions.value: drainback returns to the tank and is re-pumped (pumping energy, not lost flow); the dose count, dose volume, and float settings on the permit drawing govern

shr.formula: SHR = sensible cooling load / total cooling load. Used to select an indoor coil that matches the building's load profile.
shr.edition: ASHRAE Fundamentals by name; ACCA Manual S 2nd ed. for equipment selection.
shr.freeAccess: ACCA / ASHRAE Handbook licensed; principles free in published engineering texts.
shr.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed mechanical contractor govern. ACCA Manual J / D / S supersede rules of thumb.

wind-speed-from-velocity-pressure.formula: V = sqrt(velocity_pressure_psf / 0.00256), the ASCE 7 base velocity pressure q = 0.00256 V^2 solved for the wind speed.
wind-speed-from-velocity-pressure.edition: ASCE 7-22 (Minimum Design Loads for Buildings and Other Structures). Section 26.10 (the base 0.00256 V^2 velocity pressure), solved for V. Public formula; licensed text not reproduced.
wind-speed-from-velocity-pressure.freeAccess: ASCE 7 licensed; the 0.00256 velocity-pressure relation is public. NOAA basic wind speeds free at hazards.atcouncil.org.
wind-speed-from-velocity-pressure.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed structural engineer govern.
wind-speed-from-velocity-pressure.editionNote: The inverse of wind-pressure's base velocity pressure: the equivalent basic wind speed behind a BARE velocity pressure q. This inverts the velocity pressure only, not a Cp-loaded design surface pressure - to work back from a component/cladding or MWFRS design pressure, first divide out the exposure/height Kz, topographic Kzt, directionality Kd, gust G, and pressure Cp factors to recover q. Editions available: bundled values follow IBC 2021 and ASCE 7-22 referenced formulas. IBC 2024 is the current published edition and the one that references ASCE 7-22; IBC 2021 references ASCE 7-16, and older IBC editions reference ASCE 7-16 / 7-10. ASCE 7-22 snow is strength-level and 7-16 snow service-level, so the two are not interchangeable; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Air-density factor 0.00256
assumptions.value: ASCE 7-22 Section 26.10; V = sqrt(q / 0.00256)

assumptions.name: Bare velocity pressure
assumptions.value: enter q before Kz/Kzt/Kd/G/Cp; not a Cp-loaded design surface pressure

formwork-pressure.formula: ACI 347R wall pressure: P = C_c × C_w × (150 + 9000 × R / T) for R < 7 ft/hr and walls up to 14 ft; C_c × C_w × (150 + 43,400 / T + 2,800 × R / T) for taller walls at R < 7 or any wall at 7-15 ft/hr; full wet head above 15 ft/hr; never below 600 × C_w psf; capped at the wet-head pressure ρgh. R is pour rate (ft/hr), T is concrete temperature (°F), C_w is unit-weight coefficient.
formwork-pressure.edition: ACI 347R-14 (Guide to Formwork for Concrete) by name.
formwork-pressure.freeAccess: ACI 347 licensed; engineering-practice formulas free in published concrete texts.
formwork-pressure.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed structural engineer govern.
formwork-pressure.editionNote: Single-edition (ACI 347R-14 simplified formula; full procedure supersedes).

assumptions.name: Concrete unit weight
assumptions.value: 150 pcf normal-weight (115 / 135 for the lightweight options) unless user supplies

assumptions.name: Unit weight coefficient C_w
assumptions.value: 0.5 (1 + w/145) but not less than 0.80 below 140 pcf; 1.0 at 140-150 pcf; w/145 above 150

assumptions.name: Chemistry coefficient C_c
assumptions.value: 1.0 Type I/II/III without retarder up to 1.5 for >= 70% slag or >= 40% fly ash with retarder; an HRWR counts as a retarder

turning-clear-floor-space.formula: clear floor space 30 in x 48 in minimum, oriented so the 48 in runs toward the element on a forward approach and along it on a parallel approach. Alcove: where confinement exceeds 24 in (forward) the width must be 36 in minimum; where it exceeds 15 in (parallel) the width must be 60 in minimum. Turning space: a 60 in diameter circle, or a T within a 60 in square with arms and base 36 in wide minimum, each arm clear 12 in minimum in each direction and the base clear 24 in minimum.
turning-clear-floor-space.edition: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, 304.3.1, 304.3.2, 304.4, 305.3, 305.5, 305.7.1, and 305.7.2. A US federal standard in the public domain, quoted directly.
turning-clear-floor-space.freeAccess: The 2010 ADA Standards are published in full at no cost at ada.gov and by the US Access Board.
turning-clear-floor-space.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
turning-clear-floor-space.editionNote: These are two different spaces and they get conflated constantly. Clear floor space is where a person stands or parks in order to USE something - 30 in by 48 in. Turning space is where they turn around - a 60 in circle, or a T within a 60 in square. A room can have plenty of one and none of the other, and a compliant clear floor space is not somewhere anyone can turn around, so satisfying 305 says nothing at all about 304. The orientation of the clear floor space is the failure that gets drawn most often, because on a plan the area looks right: 305.5 requires it positioned for either a forward or a parallel approach, which means the 48 in runs toward the element on a forward approach and along it on a parallel one. Thirty by forty-eight turned the wrong way is not thirty by forty-eight. The alcove rules at 305.7 are the ones skipped entirely, and the parallel case is brutal. A clear floor space confined on three sides stops being the bare 30 x 48: a forward-approach alcove deeper than 24 in must be 36 in wide, and a PARALLEL-approach alcove deeper than 15 in must be 60 in wide - double what the bare space would have allowed, triggered by a depth barely greater than an appliance. It is why a washer squeezed between two walls fails where the same washer on an open wall passes, and the approach direction rather than the geometry decides which rule applies. The T-shaped turning space has more conditions than people remember, and it exists precisely for the rooms where 60 in of circle will not fit: within a 60 in square minimum, arms and base 36 in wide minimum, each ARM clear of obstructions 12 in minimum in each direction, and the BASE clear 24 in minimum. Doors are permitted to swing into a turning space, which is worth knowing before a layout is redrawn to avoid it. Not checked: whether a turning space or clear floor space is required at this location at all; knee and toe clearance under 306, which a T-shaped space may include at the end of the base or one arm and which changes what counts as clear; the surface and its slope, which 305.2 ties to 302 and 303; protruding objects into either space; the element being reached and its own reach ranges; door maneuvering clearances, which overlap these spaces and are governed separately; and state and local accessibility law. A space screen, not a plan review.

assumptions.name: Clear floor space
assumptions.value: 30 in minimum by 48 in minimum

assumptions.name: Orientation
assumptions.value: positioned for either forward or parallel approach; the 48 in follows the approach

assumptions.name: Forward alcove
assumptions.value: 36 in wide minimum where the depth exceeds 24 in

assumptions.name: Parallel alcove
assumptions.value: 60 in wide minimum where the depth exceeds 15 in

assumptions.name: Circular turning space
assumptions.value: 60 in diameter minimum

assumptions.name: T-shaped turning space
assumptions.value: within a 60 in square; arms and base 36 in wide; arms clear 12 in each direction; base clear 24 in

magnetic-declination.formula: Spherical-harmonic expansion of the geomagnetic potential V = a Σ_{n=1..12} (a/r)^{n+1} Σ_{m=0..n} [g_n^m cos(m λ) + h_n^m sin(m λ)] P_n^m(sin φ'); B = -∇V. WMM2025 coefficients g, h, dg/dt, dh/dt to degree 12 are bundled at data/field/wmm/coefficients.json (verbatim from NCEI WMM2025.COF). Geodetic latitude is converted to geocentric on the WGS84 ellipsoid; geocentric field components are rotated back to geodetic.
magnetic-declination.edition: NOAA NCEI World Magnetic Model 2025 (WMM2025) by name. Reference radius a = 6371.2 km; WGS84 ellipsoid (a = 6378.137 km, b = 6356.7523142 km).
magnetic-declination.freeAccess: WMM 2025 coefficients, technical report, and test-value table free at ncei.noaa.gov/products/world-magnetic-model. Coefficients are public domain (NCEI / NGA).
magnetic-declination.governance: Geometry is not forecasting. Avalanche advisory and incident commander govern.
magnetic-declination.editionNote: WMM2025 valid 2025-01-01 through 2029-12-31; coefficients expire 2030-01-01. Bundle must be refreshed at the next quinquennial release (WMM2030).

assumptions.name: Local field perturbations
assumptions.value: Solar storms, geological anomalies, and nearby ferrous gear can shift the local field by several degrees beyond the model.

window-film-shgc.formula: peak gain = area x SHGC x peak irradiance, before and after; peak reduction = the difference, and tons = that / 12000; annual = peak reduction x equivalent full-sun hours; kWh = annual BTU / EER / 1000; dollars = kWh x price; payback = area x installed cost per sq ft / dollars.
window-film-shgc.edition: The solar heat gain relation, area x SHGC x incident irradiance, and the EER definition -- cooling BTU per watt-hour of electrical input -- used to convert avoided cooling into kilowatt-hours, by name. Cooling only: the winter solar gain the film also removes is not netted out. The film manufacturer, the glass manufacturer's warranty terms, and a qualified installer govern.
window-film-shgc.freeAccess: Every term is arithmetic on user-entered values; the SHGC pair comes from the film and glazing manufacturers' published data and the irradiance and full-sun hours from local climate data.
window-film-shgc.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
window-film-shgc.editionNote: Solar heat gain coefficient is the fraction of incident solar energy that ends up as heat inside, film works by lowering it, and the saving is the difference multiplied by the glass area and by how hard the sun is hitting it. That last factor is why orientation dominates: a west exposure late on a summer afternoon is the worst case in almost every building, both because the irradiance is high and because it coincides with the peak of everything else. The two outputs answer genuinely different questions. Peak reduction in tons is a capacity argument, and a building whose cooling plant is short may avoid an equipment replacement, which makes a ton avoided at peak worth far more than a ton avoided on average. Annual kilowatt-hours is the operating argument and it converts through the equipment's EER, because dividing cooling BTU by EER gives watt-hours of electrical input -- that is what EER means. Printing the energy case honestly usually shows a long payback, which is the point: glare and fading control and freed peak capacity are the reasons most film jobs actually happen, and they should have to stand on their own rather than hide inside an energy number. The largest caveat is climate. Film lowers SHGC year-round, so in a heating-dominated climate it takes away useful winter solar gain and the annual figure here does not net that out; the true annual saving there can be near zero or negative.

assumptions.name: EER is the conversion
assumptions.value: cooling BTU divided by EER is watt-hours of electrical input, by definition

assumptions.name: Cooling only
assumptions.value: the winter solar gain the film also removes is not netted out; in a cold climate the annual saving can be negative

assumptions.name: Thermal stress not evaluated
assumptions.value: absorbing film on annealed or already-stressed glass can break it and voids many glass warranties

striping-paint-quantity.formula: stripe_sf = length_ft x width_in / 12; paint_gal = stripe_sf / coverage_sf_per_gal; beads_lb = paint_gal x bead_rate_lb_per_gal.
striping-paint-quantity.edition: Pavement-marking quantity identity by name (area from length x width; gallons from area / coverage; beads from gallons x rate); first-principles arithmetic.
striping-paint-quantity.freeAccess: The marking quantity is public quantity-survey arithmetic; the coverage and bead rate come from the marking specification.
striping-paint-quantity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
striping-paint-quantity.editionNote: The coverage (sf/gal) follows the specified wet-mil thickness - a gallon covers 1,604 sf at 1 mil, so a 15 mil line runs about 107 sf/gal and 16 mil about 100. The glass-bead drop rate is set by the retroreflectivity spec. A skip (dashed) line applies a duty-cycle fraction of the length. Distinct from architectural wall-paint coverage.

assumptions.name: Coverage
assumptions.value: ~100 sf/gal default for a 16 wet mil line; the marking spec's thickness governs

assumptions.name: Bead rate
assumptions.value: ~6 lb/gal default; set by the retroreflectivity spec

cable-reel-capacity.formula: length_ft = fill_factor x PI x (flange_dia_in^2 - drum_dia_in^2) x traverse_width_in / (48 x cable_od_in^2).
cable-reel-capacity.edition: Reel-capacity identity by name (annular winding volume / cable cross-section, with a fill factor); first-principles geometry.
cable-reel-capacity.freeAccess: The reel-capacity geometry is public first-principles; the reel dimensions come from the reel and the cable OD from the cable.
cable-reel-capacity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
cable-reel-capacity.editionNote: The fill factor accounts for imperfect winding (about 0.85-0.9). The same relation works backward to read the length left on a partial reel from the measured buildup. The reel dimensions come from the reel and the cable OD from the cable.

assumptions.name: Fill factor
assumptions.value: ~0.85-0.9 for imperfect winding; the winding pattern governs

assumptions.name: Cable OD
assumptions.value: the cable outside diameter; it enters squared, so a fatter cable cuts the reel sharply

bearing-l10-life.formula: p = 3 (ball) or 10/3 (roller); L10 = (C/P)^p x 10^6 rev; L10h = L10 / (60 x rpm).
bearing-l10-life.edition: The ISO 281 / ABMA 9 & 11 basic rating life (L10) of a rolling-element bearing, by name; the mounting, lubrication, and application govern.
bearing-l10-life.freeAccess: The L10 rating-life relation is a published ISO 281 / ABMA result; the dynamic load rating C comes from the bearing catalog and the equivalent load P from the application.
bearing-l10-life.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
bearing-l10-life.editionNote: ISO 281 basic rating life. L10 = (C/P)^p x 10^6 revolutions and L10h = L10 / (60 x rpm) hours, with p = 3 for ball bearings and 10/3 for roller bearings. Life scales as the cube (ball) of the load ratio, so a modest overload cuts life sharply (a 25% overload roughly halves it) and a small load reduction buys a large life gain. The basic L10 assumes clean, well-lubricated operation; contamination, misalignment, and lubricant condition are handled by the modified aISO life. L10 is the life at which 10% of a population has failed, not the average. A planning estimate, not a warranty; the mounting, lubrication, and application govern.

assumptions.name: Cube law
assumptions.value: life scales as (C/P)^3 for ball bearings, (C/P)^(10/3) for roller

assumptions.name: Basic L10
assumptions.value: assumes clean, well-lubricated operation; contamination needs the modified aISO life

assumptions.name: 10% definition
assumptions.value: L10 is the life at which 10% have failed, not the average (L50 is ~5x)

thread-pitch.formula: Inch: P = 1 / TPI. Metric: P is the pitch in mm, TPI = 25.4 / P. Lead = P * starts. Sharp-V 60-degree height H = P * cos(30) = P * sqrt(3) / 2.
thread-pitch.edition: Thread pitch, lead, and 60-degree form - Unified (UN/UNC/UNF) inch and ISO metric threads share a 60-degree included angle - as in Machinery's Handbook (Industrial Press), by name; first-principles geometry.
thread-pitch.freeAccess: Pure geometry, public; the truncated thread depth and the tap-drill size are thread-form- and class-specific and are not computed here.
thread-pitch.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
thread-pitch.editionNote: First-principles 60-degree thread geometry. The lead (axial advance per turn) equals the pitch on a single-start thread and a multiple of it on a multi-start thread; the sharp-V height is the theoretical fundamental triangle, not the truncated working depth.

assumptions.name: Thread form
assumptions.value: 60-degree included angle (UN/UNC/UNF and ISO metric); Acme, buttress, and pipe-thread forms are not covered

weld-transverse-shrinkage.formula: Transverse shrinkage per weld = 0.2 x weld area / thickness + 0.05 x root opening (the coefficients are dimensionless; the area-over-thickness ratio carries the length); total = per-weld x weld count; recommended pre-set = total.
weld-transverse-shrinkage.edition: Transverse weld shrinkage - the Blodgett weld-area-over-thickness relation from Blodgett, Design of Welded Structures (James F. Lincoln Arc Welding Foundation), by name.
weld-transverse-shrinkage.freeAccess: The published Blodgett relation; the weld area, thickness, and weld count are user-supplied.
weld-transverse-shrinkage.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
weld-transverse-shrinkage.editionNote: Blodgett transverse-shrinkage relation shrink = 0.2 x A_w / t + 0.05 d (d the root opening). This is a screen: joint restraint, fixturing, sequence, and a mock-up govern the actual movement, and longitudinal and angular distortion (restraint-dominated) are out of scope.

assumptions.name: Blodgett coefficient
assumptions.value: 0.2 (dimensionless); fixed in the compute

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: transverse component only; longitudinal and angular distortion not estimated

gutter-downspout.formula: Adjusted area = plan area x pitch factor x (rainfall / 5 in/hr); downspouts = ceil((adjusted / 100) / downspout sq in); gutter design area = plan area x pitch factor x rainfall (in/hr): 5 in K-style up to 5,520, 6 in K-style up to 7,960, else split the run or go larger.
gutter-downspout.edition: SMACNA / standard residential gutter method (by name).
gutter-downspout.freeAccess: SMACNA licensed; rainfall intensity free from NOAA Atlas 14 at hdsc.nws.noaa.gov.
gutter-downspout.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
gutter-downspout.editionNote: Single-edition (engineering-practice / first-principles take-off; refresh as practice and product data shift).

assumptions.name: Reference intensity
assumptions.value: 5 in/hr reference; 1 sq in of downspout per ~100 sq ft of roof (editable)

deck-board-takeoff.formula: boards = ceil((deck_width_ft x 12 + gap_in) / (board_face_in + gap_in)); lineal_ft = boards x deck_length_ft x (1 + waste_pct/100); joists = ceil(deck_length_ft x 12 / joist_spacing_in) + 1; screws = boards x joists x 2.
deck-board-takeoff.edition: First-principles deck-surface takeoff (the same carpentry take-off basis as fence-estimate and residential-framing), by name; the deck plan and the lumber on the rack govern.
deck-board-takeoff.freeAccess: First-principles arithmetic; no proprietary source reproduced. The board width, gap, spacing, and waste come from the deck plan and the product.
deck-board-takeoff.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
deck-board-takeoff.editionNote: Deck surface takeoff: the boards run the length, so the count across the width is ceil((width + gap) / (board face + gap)) -- the gap falls between boards, not after the last. Lineal feet = boards x length x (1 + waste); butt joints must land on a joist and are staggered, and the waste covers cutoffs, culls, and crook. The joists carrying the deck run across the width at the given spacing, so their count along the length is ceil(length x 12 / spacing) + 1, and two deck screws (or hidden clips) per board at every joist gives boards x joists x 2 fasteners. Sizes the surface and fasteners only, not the joists, beam, posts, or footings, which come from the span tables and the load. A takeoff estimate, not a structural design.

assumptions.name: Gap placement
assumptions.value: the gap falls between boards, not after the last: boards = ceil((width + gap) / (face + gap))

assumptions.name: Fastener count
assumptions.value: two deck screws per board at every joist crossing (hidden clips are one system per board per joist)

track-warp-fra-class.formula: warp = |cross level at A - cross level at B| (49 CFR 213.63(a), the raw readings); split into designed change = designed A - designed B and deviation twist = (measured A - designed A) - (measured B - designed B); pass when warp <= the entered limit; margin = entered limit - warp; the same twist scaled to a 31 ft base = absolute warp x 31 / distance.
track-warp-fra-class.edition: 49 CFR 213.63(a) (as amended at 91 FR 22735, April 28, 2026): warp is the difference in cross level between any two points less than 62 ft apart; 213.59(b) holds spiral runoff to the same limits. 49 CFR 213 is named as the source of the limits by class of track. The limit tables are not reproduced; the applicable limit is entered. The qualified track inspector and the track owner govern.
track-warp-fra-class.freeAccess: 49 CFR 213 is US federal regulation and public domain; this is subtraction on the user's own level-board readings against a limit they supply.
track-warp-fra-class.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
track-warp-fra-class.editionNote: Warp is a twist, and a twist unloads a wheel. A rigid truck bridging a section of track that rises on one rail and falls on the other has one wheel carrying much less than its share, and a lightly loaded wheel on a curve with lateral force is the wheel that climbs. That is the derailment mechanism, and it is why warp limits tighten faster with class than most other parameters. The measurement detail that decides what a reading means is the reference. FRA warp is the raw difference in cross level between the two points: on a curve of constant elevation the superelevation cancels out of it, while on a spiral the designed runoff stays in it, because the wheel feels planned twist and unplanned twist alike, and 213.59(b) holds the runoff to the same limits. Until 2026-10-01 this tile judged only the deviation from the designed cross level, which passed a spiral reading 2.04 in of cross-level change against a 1.5 in limit. The deviation share is still reported, because it is the part surfacing can fix. The reading also has to be paired with the measurement length, since the rule is written per 62 ft and the pre-1998 spiral exception per 31 ft, which is why the same twist is reported on both bases here. The FRA limit tables themselves are set by class and by parameter in the adopted regulation and are not shipped.

assumptions.name: Warp is the raw cross-level difference
assumptions.value: the designed runoff on a spiral counts toward the limit; constant superelevation cancels out

assumptions.name: Measurement length matters
assumptions.value: 31 ft and 62 ft warp carry different limits; the length must be stated with the reading

assumptions.name: Limits are entered, not shipped
assumptions.value: the class limits are set by the adopted regulation and must come from it

screen-deck-capacity.formula: capacity TPH = screen area x base capacity for the opening x the PRODUCT of the oversize, halfsize, deck position, wet screening and efficiency factors; the area a feed requires = feed rate / (base capacity x the combined multiplier).
screen-deck-capacity.edition: The multiplicative factor method by name. Every factor and the base capacity come from the screen manufacturer's published tables, differ between manufacturers and media types, and are entered rather than shipped. The manufacturer's selection data and the plant designer govern.
screen-deck-capacity.freeAccess: Multiplication on factors the user reads off the manufacturer's tables; no capacity table is reproduced.
screen-deck-capacity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
screen-deck-capacity.editionNote: Every factor in the chain is a departure from a reference condition, and the chain is multiplicative, so the errors compound rather than average. The two that dominate are the halfsize and oversize factors: a feed with a lot of material smaller than half the opening screens far faster than the base rate, and a feed sitting right at the opening size screens far slower. That is why a screen comfortable on one gradation blinds and floods on another from the same pit, and why tightening a crusher upstream can cost a deck a third of its capacity without anyone touching the screen. For field use the important output is not the capacity number but the comparison against what the deck is actually being fed. A deck running above its calculated capacity carries a bed too deep for particles to reach the wire, and the symptom is oversize in the product with no mechanical fault anywhere -- the screen is working correctly and is simply out of area. Knowing that stops a crew from chasing stroke, slope, and wire tension for a problem none of them can fix. This does not size the drive, select stroke, speed, slope, or media, or evaluate blinding and pegging, which are material-property problems no capacity formula predicts.

assumptions.name: The factors multiply, so errors compound
assumptions.value: and the halfsize and oversize factors dominate the chain

assumptions.name: Oversize with no fault is an AREA problem
assumptions.value: the bed is too deep for particles to reach the wire

assumptions.name: A tighter crusher can starve a screen
assumptions.value: fewer fines is a lower halfsize factor and a large capacity loss

temporary-stairway-check.formula: angle = atan(riser height / tread depth) in degrees, required between 30 and 50; a stairrail is required where risers >= 4 OR total rise > 30 in (whichever comes first); uniformity passes where the worst of the riser-height and tread-depth variations is <= 1/4 in; stairrail height >= 36 in from its upper surface to the tread surface; landing depth >= 30 in in the direction of travel.
temporary-stairway-check.edition: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1052, Subpart X - Stairways and Ladders. A US federal regulation in the public domain, quoted directly.
temporary-stairway-check.freeAccess: 29 CFR is published in full at no cost by OSHA and the eCFR.
temporary-stairway-check.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
temporary-stairway-check.editionNote: Three things separate a construction stairway from a finished one. The stairrail trigger is a double condition phrased in a way that reads backwards at first: four or more risers OR rising more than 30 inches, WHICHEVER IS LESS. Whichever is less means whichever comes FIRST, so either condition alone catches the flight - a three-riser flight climbing 32 in is caught by the rise despite failing the riser count, and a four-riser flight climbing 24 in is caught by the count despite failing the rise. Reading it as requiring both is the common error and it exempts flights the standard covers. The angle is bounded on BOTH sides, between 30 and 50 degrees from horizontal, and too shallow is a violation rather than a courtesy: a run under 30 degrees is a ramp with steps in it, and people trip on it precisely because it does not read as stairs from above. Uniformity is the third: riser height and tread depth uniform within each flight, with variation not over 1/4 inch in any stairway system. That is a variation ACROSS the flight rather than a tolerance on each step, so a flight of individually reasonable steps still fails if the first and last differ by more than a quarter inch - and the step people fall on is the odd one, not the average one. Not checked: the 22 in landing width; handrail height and clearance, which differ from the stairrail figures; midrails and the openings between them; whether a stairway is required at all rather than a ladder or ramp; the prohibition on using stairs with unfilled metal pan treads; temporary treads and landings during construction; spiral and alternating tread devices; and finished-stair geometry, which is a different code entirely and has its own tiles. A screen, not a stair design; Subpart X and the competent person govern.

assumptions.name: Angle
assumptions.value: between 30 and 50 degrees from horizontal - bounded both ways

assumptions.name: Stairrail trigger
assumptions.value: four or more risers OR rising more than 30 in, whichever comes first

assumptions.name: Stairrail height
assumptions.value: not less than 36 in from the upper surface to the tread, post-1991

assumptions.name: Uniformity
assumptions.value: variation not over 1/4 in ACROSS the flight, not per step

assumptions.name: Landing depth
assumptions.value: not less than 30 in in the direction of travel, at every 12 ft or less of rise

assumptions.name: Not checked
assumptions.value: landing width, handrails, midrails, metal pan treads, spiral and alternating treads

ballnose-scallop-height.formula: scallop mode: h = R - sqrt(R^2 - (s/2)^2); stepover mode: s = 2 sqrt(R^2 - (R - h)^2); approx h ~ s^2/(8R).
ballnose-scallop-height.edition: The ballnose scallop (cusp) height geometry and its inverse, with the small-scallop approximation, as compiled in the CAM and mold-machining references, by name.
ballnose-scallop-height.freeAccess: The ballnose scallop-height geometry is a public CAM/milling result in the standard machining references.
ballnose-scallop-height.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
ballnose-scallop-height.editionNote: The ballnose scallop height h = R - sqrt(R^2 - (s/2)^2) and its inverse s = 2 sqrt(R^2 - (R - h)^2), with the small-scallop approximation h ~ s^2/(8R), as compiled in the CAM / mold-machining references. This returns the theoretical scallop between parallel passes on a flat surface - it is the geometric cusp (a sloped surface changes the effective stepover, and tool deflection and runout add to the real finish), assumes a true ballnose radius, and does not cover the cusp along the feed direction (that is the feed/turning-surface-finish geometry) or convert to Ra. A shop aid; the actual finish depends on the tool, deflection, and surface slope.

assumptions.name: Scallop geometry
assumptions.value: h = R - sqrt(R^2 - (s/2)^2) between parallel passes of a ballnose radius R

assumptions.name: s^2 scaling
assumptions.value: near the bottom h ~ s^2/(8R), so doubling the stepover quadruples the scallop

assumptions.name: Flat, geometric
assumptions.value: theoretical cusp on a flat surface; slope, deflection, and runout change the real finish

rc-doubly-reinforced.formula: a = (As - A's) fy / (0.85 f'c b); c = a/beta1; eps's = 0.003 (c - d')/c; eps_t = 0.003 (d - c)/c; Mn = (As - A's) fy (d - a/2) + A's fy (d - d'); phi Mn (phi = 0.90 tension-controlled).
rc-doubly-reinforced.edition: The ACI 318-19 doubly-reinforced rectangular-beam flexural capacity with the compression-steel yield check and the tension-controlled strength-reduction factor, by name.
rc-doubly-reinforced.freeAccess: ACI 318 is readable free through the ACI online reading room at concrete.org; the flexural provisions are in the published code.
rc-doubly-reinforced.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
rc-doubly-reinforced.editionNote: The ACI 318-19 doubly-reinforced rectangular-beam capacity a = (As - A's) fy / (0.85 f'c b), Mn = (As - A's) fy (d - a/2) + A's fy (d - d'), the compression-steel yield check epsilon's = 0.003 (c - d')/c >= fy/Es, and the ACI 318-19 21.2.2 strength-reduction factor: tension-controlled phi = 0.90 at epsilon_t >= epsilon_ty + 0.003, 0.65 at epsilon_t <= epsilon_ty = fy/Es, linear between. This assumes both steel layers yield (flagged when the compression steel does not, where a rigorous solution would iterate with f's = Es epsilon's <= fy), covers a rectangular section (no T-beam flange), and does not check minimum steel, bar spacing, or development. A design aid, not a substitute for the structural engineer of record's stamped design.

assumptions.name: Two couples
assumptions.value: the singly-reinforced concrete couple plus the compression-steel-to-tension-steel couple A's fy (d - d')

assumptions.name: Both yield
assumptions.value: both steel layers are assumed at fy; the compression-steel strain is checked and flagged

assumptions.name: Tension-controlled
assumptions.value: phi = 0.90 at epsilon_t >= epsilon_ty + 0.003 (the 318-19 limit, not the fixed 0.005); transition below

concrete-cracking-moment.formula: fr = 7.5 x lambda x sqrt(f'c); S = b h^2 / 6; Mcr = fr x S (= fr Ig/yt); Mcr_kipft = Mcr_lbin / 12000.
concrete-cracking-moment.edition: The ACI 318-19 cracking moment Mcr = fr Ig/yt with the 19.2.3.1 modulus of rupture, by name.
concrete-cracking-moment.freeAccess: ACI 318 is readable free through the ACI online reading room at concrete.org; the cracking-moment and 19.2.3 rupture provisions are in the published code.
concrete-cracking-moment.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
concrete-cracking-moment.editionNote: The ACI 318-19 cracking moment Mcr = fr Ig/yt, the bending moment at which a plain (uncracked) section first cracks in flexure. With the modulus of rupture fr = 7.5 x lambda x sqrt(f'c) psi (19.2.3.1; lambda 1.0 normalweight, 0.75 all-lightweight) and the gross rectangular section modulus S = Ig/yt = b h^2/6, Mcr = fr b h^2/6. This is the value behind the effective-moment-of-inertia (Ie) deflection analysis and the minimum-flexural-reinforcement check (the design flexural strength must reach at least 1.2 Mcr). It uses the gross rectangular section with the reinforcement transform neglected (the standard approximation); a T-beam or a heavily reinforced section uses the transformed gross moment of inertia. A design aid, not a substitute for the structural engineer of record's stamped design.

assumptions.name: Cracking moment
assumptions.value: Mcr = fr Ig/yt = fr b h^2/6 for a gross rectangular section

assumptions.name: Rupture stress
assumptions.value: fr = 7.5 x lambda x sqrt(f'c) psi (lambda 1.0 NW, 0.75 LW)

assumptions.name: Gross section
assumptions.value: reinforcement transform neglected; a T-beam uses the transformed Ig

fresh-concrete-temp.formula: T = [0.22(Ta x Wa + Tc x Wc) + Tw x Ww + Ta x Wwa] / [0.22(Wa + Wc) + Ww + Wwa]; solids specific heat 0.22 Btu/lb-F, water 1.0, aggregate free moisture at the aggregate temperature.
fresh-concrete-temp.edition: ACI 305.1 Specification for Hot Weather Concreting (the batch heat-balance for fresh concrete temperature); PCA Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures, by name; the mix design and project specification govern.
fresh-concrete-temp.freeAccess: The mass-weighted heat balance is first-principles; the 0.22 solids specific heat is the standard ACI value. Ingredient weights and temperatures come from the batch ticket.
fresh-concrete-temp.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
fresh-concrete-temp.editionNote: ACI 305.1 fresh-concrete temperature by heat balance: the mix temperature is the mass-weighted average of its ingredients, weighting the solids (cement and aggregate) by their specific heat ~0.22 Btu/lb-F and water by 1.0, so T = [0.22(Ta Wa + Tc Wc) + Tw Ww + Twa Wwa] / [0.22(Wa + Wc) + Ww + Wwa]. Because water's heat capacity is over four times the solids', the mix water is the cheapest lever -- chilling it, or replacing part of it with ice (crediting the 144 Btu/lb heat of fusion), pulls the batch down the most per pound. The aggregate, the largest mass, sets the baseline, and its free surface moisture rides at the aggregate temperature. Hot-weather concreting (ACI 305) commonly caps the placing temperature near 90 F; above it, set time shortens, slump loss and plastic-shrinkage cracking rise, and 28-day strength can drop. Cement heat of hydration and mixer friction add a few degrees this static balance omits. A batching aid, not the mix design.

assumptions.name: Specific heats
assumptions.value: solids (cement + aggregate) ~0.22 Btu/lb-F, water 1.0; aggregate free moisture at the aggregate temperature

assumptions.name: Omits
assumptions.value: cement heat of hydration and mixer friction, which add a few degrees

glulam-volume-factor.formula: Cv = min( (21/L)^(1/x) x (12/d)^(1/x) x (5.125/b)^(1/x), 1.0 ), L between points of zero moment; allowable bending uses the lesser of Cv and CL. The optional KL multiplier (default 1.0) is the NDS 1997 loading factor, absent from the current NDS.
glulam-volume-factor.edition: NDS 2018 (National Design Specification for Wood Construction) §5.3.6, the glulam volume factor Cv, by name; the reference bending value and factors come from the NDS Supplement.
glulam-volume-factor.freeAccess: The Cv equation is stated in NDS 5.3.6, published free read-only by AWC at awc.org; the (21/L)^(1/x) arithmetic is public.
glulam-volume-factor.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
glulam-volume-factor.editionNote: NDS 2018 §5.3.6 gives the glued-laminated volume factor Cv = (21/L)^(1/x) x (12/d)^(1/x) x (5.125/b)^(1/x), capped at 1.0, where L is the length between points of zero moment in feet, d and b the depth and width in inches, and x = 10 for all species except Southern Pine (x = 20). The loading-condition factor KL of NDS 1997 is not in the current equation; the tile keeps it as an optional multiplier that defaults to 1.0. Until 2026-09-26 this note credited KL to NDS 2018. A larger stressed volume is more likely to contain a strength-limiting defect, so the reference bending value Fb is reduced. The allowable bending value uses the LESSER of Cv and the beam-stability factor CL (NDS 3.3.3) - they are not multiplied together. Cv applies to glulam bending about the x-x (strong) axis, not to sawn lumber and not to weak-axis bending. A design aid, not a substitute for the engineer of record.

assumptions.name: Volume factor
assumptions.value: Cv = (21/L)^(1/x) x (12/d)^(1/x) x (5.125/b)^(1/x), capped at 1.0; L between points of zero moment

assumptions.name: Species exponent
assumptions.value: x = 10 for all species except Southern Pine, where x = 20

assumptions.name: Lesser of Cv or CL
assumptions.value: the allowable bending uses the lesser of Cv and the stability factor CL, not their product

weld-visual-acceptance.formula: a crack is rejectable WITHOUT regard to size; undersize is two independent tests -- the amount against a permitted allowance and the length against a permitted fraction of the weld, both of which must pass; undercut is compared against a limit that differs between statically and cyclically loaded connections.
weld-visual-acceptance.edition: Weld visual acceptance as AWS D1.1 and equivalent codes structure it. Every limit is ENTERED from the applicable code and edition, because an acceptance table reproduced here would go stale between editions and be wrong for every code but the one chosen.
weld-visual-acceptance.freeAccess: Comparisons against entered limits; no code table is reproduced.
weld-visual-acceptance.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
weld-visual-acceptance.editionNote: Three things decide a visual examination and they fail differently, which is why they are kept apart. A CRACK is rejectable without dimension, and nothing else is reached once one is found -- the one most often argued about is the crater crack at a stop, which is small, looks cosmetic, and is a crack. UNDERSIZE is two tests: a limited amount over a limited length, both of which must be satisfied, so a weld a sixteenth light over a short run can be acceptable while the same shortfall over the whole weld is not. And the limits themselves depend on the LOADING -- undercut allowances tighten and porosity criteria change between static and cyclic connections, so the same weld can pass as one and fail as the other, and on a structure carrying both the criteria change from member to member.

assumptions.name: Limits are entered per code and edition
assumptions.value: no acceptance table is reproduced
assumptions.source: AWS D1.1 or the applicable code

assumptions.name: Loading must be known first
assumptions.value: static and cyclic criteria differ

assumptions.name: A subset of visual items
assumptions.value: reinforcement, convexity, overlap, profile and arc strikes are not covered

drone-gsd-overlap.formula: GSD = flight height x sensor pixel pitch / focal length; the image footprint is GSD x the sensor pixel dimensions; line spacing = footprint width x (1 - side overlap); shot interval = footprint height x (1 - forward overlap); image count = area / (line spacing x shot interval).
drone-gsd-overlap.edition: The photogrammetric ground sample distance relation by name. GSD IS RESOLUTION, NOT ACCURACY: accuracy comes from ground control, camera calibration and block geometry, and is not computed here. Nadir imagery over level ground; terrain relief varies both the GSD and the overlap across a frame. Airspace, authorisation and visual line of sight are outside it. The applicable civil aviation rules, the project's accuracy specification, and the surveyor of record govern.
drone-gsd-overlap.freeAccess: One similar-triangles ratio on numbers off a camera spec sheet; no flight planning software output is reproduced.
drone-gsd-overlap.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
drone-gsd-overlap.editionNote: GSD scales linearly with height and the cost of improving it does not: HALVING THE HEIGHT HALVES THE GSD AND QUADRUPLES THE IMAGE COUNT, because both footprint dimensions halve at once -- four times the flight time, the battery swaps, and processing that scales worse than linearly. The most important sentence in the subject is that GSD is not accuracy: a survey flown at half a centimetre per pixel with no ground control can be metres out and will look magnificent while it is wrong. Overlap goes HIGHER over vegetation, water and uniform surfaces, because matching needs texture, and a flight planned at minimum overlap over canopy leaves holes no processing recovers.

assumptions.name: Image count is area-only
assumptions.value: area / (line spacing x shot interval); a flight plan adds a line and two images beyond each end of every line (Penn State GEOG 892: lines = width / spacing + 1, images per line = length / base + 1 + 4), so the real count runs higher on a small site

assumptions.name: GSD is resolution, not accuracy
assumptions.value: accuracy comes from ground control and block geometry

assumptions.name: Nadir over level ground
assumptions.value: terrain relief varies the GSD and overlap across the frame

assumptions.name: Airspace and authorisation are outside it
assumptions.value: and they govern whether the flight happens

mast-climber-platform-load.formula: utilization against the platform's total rating and against the ZONE rating for the load's position; the moment about the mast = load x distance; the tie force = that moment divided by the mast tie spacing.
mast-climber-platform-load.edition: The cantilever load-distribution relations by name. ZONE RATINGS ARE THE MANUFACTURER'S and are entered: cantilever ends carry a small fraction of the platform's rating, and a load within the total can exceed a zone. It does not compute wind load, mast capacity, erected height limits, or tie anchorage into the structure. The manufacturer's load chart and erection manual, the competent person, and the erector's engineering govern.
mast-climber-platform-load.freeAccess: Two ratios and one moment on ratings the reader takes from the load chart; no chart is reproduced.
mast-climber-platform-load.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
mast-climber-platform-load.editionNote: A mast climber is a CANTILEVER, and the manufacturer's capacity is stated for a defined load distribution. Placing the same total at the outboard edge produces a moment the platform and mast were never rated for even though the scale says the load is within capacity -- which is why manufacturers publish load charts by ZONE rather than as a single figure. Masonry work is the case that stresses it: a platform staged with cubes of block by a forklift at whatever spot is accessible can exceed a zone's rating while the total stays comfortably under. The mast ties are where the moment ends up, so the tie pattern is part of the load path and not an incidental -- and ties anchored into cladding rather than structure are the failure no load chart can see.

assumptions.name: Zone ratings are the manufacturer's
assumptions.value: they differ between machines and configurations

assumptions.name: No wind load
assumptions.value: on the platform or on any sheeting

assumptions.name: No mast or anchorage capacity
assumptions.value: the base, foundation and tie anchorage are separate

storm-panel-plywood.formula: panel = opening + 2 x overlap each way; span = dimension between the fastened edges (<= 8 ft); thickness >= 7/16 in; fasteners per edge = ceil((edge length - 2 x edge distance) / spacing) + 1, x 2 edges; sheets by nesting onto 4 x 8 ft stock; spacing entered from the adopted Table R301.2.1.2 column for the span.
storm-panel-plywood.edition: IRC Section R301.2.1.2 and its exception for wood structural panels, and Table R301.2.1.2 (2018 edition limited to a 45 ft mean roof height and 180 mph Vult), cited by section; the fastening schedule is NOT reproduced. The adopted IRC and the AHJ govern.
storm-panel-plywood.freeAccess: The IRC is cited by section only; the fastener spacing is a user input read from the adopted edition's table.
storm-panel-plywood.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
storm-panel-plywood.editionNote: Board-up protection works only if the panel reaches the framing and the fasteners hold it there. The exception permits plywood or OSB at least 7/16 in thick spanning no more than 8 ft, precut, predrilled, and attached to the framing around the opening, fastened at two opposing edges with the spacing tightening as the span grows. Fastening the long sides keeps the span short and usually the fastener schedule lighter. A panel larger than a 4 x 8 sheet needs a splice the exception does not provide. The table applies only within its height and wind-speed limits, and earlier editions used a lower height limit, so the adopted edition matters.

assumptions.name: Panel minimums
assumptions.value: wood structural panel at least 7/16 in thick, span not over 8 ft

assumptions.name: Fastener spacing
assumptions.value: entered from the adopted Table R301.2.1.2 for the fastener type and span

assumptions.name: Sheet stock
assumptions.value: identical panels nested onto 48 x 96 in sheets, no splicing
